extracted.intended_audience: poets and playwrights composing tragedy; students of dramatic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and evaluative principles for composing tragic poetry/drama (plot, character, recognition, diction, chorus, episodes, and performance). Focuses on what makes a successful tragedy and common faults to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: goodness
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should be good (not necessarily perfect), since goodness is the first thing to aim at in portraiture of character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even a woman may be good, and also a slave; but some roles (e.g., a slave) are 'absolutely bad' in Aristotle's taxonomy. Use goodness as a guiding evaluative trait when shaping characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: propriety (fitness to sex/class/role)
rubrics_metrics.description: Portrayal must observe propriety — characters should exhibit traits appropriate to their sex, station, or role (e.g., 'there is a type of manly valour; but for a woman to be valiant in this sense would be inappropriate').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid incongruous or inappropriate behavior for a character's social/natural role (anti-pattern examples: a woman behaving with male-typical manliness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: truth to life (probability/naturalness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Character must be true to life — distinct from mere goodness or propriety; characters should act and speak in ways that are probable and lifelike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet should preserve the type while making it lifelike and ennobled (example: Achilles as portrayed by Agathon and Homer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: consistency (even consistent inconsistency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters must be consistent: even if the original character type is inconsistent, the depiction must be 'consistently inconsistent'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid gratuitous changes of personality across a work (anti-pattern example: Iphigenia in Aulis who later does not resemble her earlier self).

rubrics_metrics.name: Action must follow necessity or probability
rubrics_metrics.description: A person of a given character should speak or act by the rule either of necessity or of probability; events should follow by necessary or probable sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both speeches and plot events must be causally or probabilistically justified; improbable or unmotivated acts weaken credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot solutions must arise from the plot, not from 'machinery'
rubrics_metrics.description: Travelling of the plot and its resolutions must be brought about by the plot itself, and not by external machinery (e.g., deus ex machina).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Machinery (divine sight, miracles) is only legitimate for events external to the drama (previous to it or subsequent and needing announcement). Within the action there must be nothing irrational; if irrationality cannot be excluded it should be placed outside the scope of the tragedy (example: the irrational element in Sophocles' Oedipus belongs to the wider story).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet should ennoble types (imitate good portrait-painters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Like portrait-painters reproducing the distinctive form and making a likeness 'true to life and yet more beautiful', the poet should preserve types and 'ennoble' them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent defects (quick or slow to anger, etc.) so that the type is preserved yet rendered more admirable; examples: portrayals of Achilles by Agathon and Homer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to sensory concomitants (but not essential)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals to the senses are concomitants of poetry and, though not essential, should not be neglected; there is much room for error in their handling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sensory detail appropriately but avoid letting such appeals substitute for proper plot and character work; earlier treatises expand on these matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (anagnorisis): forms and artistic ranking
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition has kinds: by signs/tokens, by turn of fortune, by poet-invented disclosure, by memory (sight or sound), and by process of reasoning. They vary in artistic merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rankings/examples: (1) recognition by signs/tokens (scars, necklaces) is inartistic or less artistic; (2) recognition resulting from change of fortune (e.g., Odyssey bath scene) is better; (3) recognitions invented at will by the poet (characters simply stating facts not required by plot) are lacking in art; (4) memory-triggered recognition (sight of a picture, music) is good; (5) recognition by reasoning is acceptable; (6) best of all is recognition arising from incidents themselves producing a startling/probable effect (examples: Oedipus and Iphigenia).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid poet-invented recognitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognitions invented at the poet's whim (e.g., a character saying what the poet wants rather than what the plot requires) are nearly allied to the fault of token-based recognition and are deemed unartistic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer recognitions that are motivated by plot conditions rather than gratuitous revelations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place the scene vividly before the mind's eye
rubrics_metrics.description: When constructing and working out the plot and language, the poet should place the scene, as far as possible, before his eyes to see everything with utmost vividness and thus detect inconsistencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visualizing the action as if one were a spectator helps to discover what is in keeping with the action and reduces oversight (example: Carcinus' oversight of Amphiaraus leaving the sanctuary offended the audience).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate gestures and stagecraft
rubrics_metrics.description: Work out the play with appropriate gestures; those who feel emotion are most impressive by force of sympathy. One who is agitated storms; one who is angry rages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gestures and embodiment of passions add lifelike reality; these are part of the poet's responsibility in staging scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sketch general outline first, then fill episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: In shaping subjects (traditional or new), first sketch the general outline of the play, then fill in the episodes and amplify in detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Iphigenia — general plan: sacrifice, disappearance, transportation, later brother arrives; the oracle's reason may be outside the action proper. Episodes should be arranged to be appropriate to the general plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episodes must be relevant and proportioned (short in drama)
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodes must be relevant to the action; in drama episodes are short and give extension to epic poem, but should not overwhelm the drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure episodes relate to and serve the main action (example: Odyssey's many episodes are suitable for epic length but would over-extend a drama).

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of tragedy: complication and unravelling (peripeteia and catastrophe)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy divides into two parts—Complication (from beginning to turning point) and Unravelling/Denouement (from beginning of the change to the end).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Complication includes incidents presupposed in the drama and portion of action proper that marks the turning point from good to bad fortune or vice versa; the Unravelling resolves consequences to the end. Maintain clarity of these divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of tragedy and aim to combine merits
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four kinds of tragedy: the Complicated (reversal and recognition), the Simple, the Pathetic (motive = passion), and the Ethical (motive = character/ethos). (Supernatural types may be excluded.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet should, if possible, combine poetic merits or at least the most important ones; critics expect excellence across several lines, not narrow specialization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot identity defined by complication and unravelling
rubrics_metrics.description: When judging whether tragedies are the same or different, the best test is the plot: identity exists where both Complication and Unravelling are the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many poets knot (complicate) well but unravel badly; both skills must be mastered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid epic multiplicity of plots in drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not make a tragedy into an epic structure (avoid multiplicity of plots as in attempting to dramatize the entire Iliad); drama requires selection and unity of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic length permits parts to assume proper magnitude; in drama, excess multiplicity causes failure (examples: failures of poets who dramatized whole Iliad or Niobe).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus as integral actor
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus should be regarded as one of the actors: an integral part of the whole and should share in the action (as in Sophocles), not act as disconnected interludes (as in some later poets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid choral songs that pertain as little to the subject as to any other tragedy; that practice turns choral parts into mere interludes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (dianoia): speeches must produce rhetorical effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought encompasses the effects to be produced by speech — proof and refutation, excitation of feelings such as pity, fear, anger, and the heightening or extenuating of facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic incidents should be treated from the same points of view as dramatic speeches when the object is to evoke pity, fear, grandeur, or probability; design speeches to achieve these effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show, don't merely tell: incidents should speak for themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: Incidents should ideally speak for themselves without verbal exposition; the effects aimed at in a speech should be produced by the speaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the impression can be conveyed directly by the incident, the speech is redundant. Use language to produce effects where incidents cannot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction and figures of speech belong to declamation
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures of speech and the classification of command, prayer, narrative, threat, question, answer, etc., belong more properly to the art of Declamation than to poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge of these figures is not a severe criterion for poetic censure; specialists in declamation handle fine rhetorical categories, though the poet should be broadly aware.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to phonetics and metrical properties (letters, syllables, connecting words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Language components (letters, syllables, connecting words, nouns, verbs, inflexions, sentences) and phonetic distinctions (vowels, semi-vowels, mutes; long/short; acute/grave) affect diction and metre and must be considered by metrical treatises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet or metrists should be attentive to how sounds and syllables form meter, e.g., which letters make syllables, types of non-significant connecting words, and syllabic composition relevant to metre.
